From the Morning Courier and New York Enquirer, January 9, 1841.

The Packet ship Oarrick. þÿ Our ship news Collector has furnished us with the following intelligence concerning this vessel. She went on shore at 4, A M., on Thursday, twenty miles south of the Highlands. A few minutes before she struck, she had ten fathoms water, and was in the act of wearing when she struck. At day light, all the passengers with their baggage and the crew, were landed safe on the beach, and arrived in the city last night in the steamboat Osiris, Captain Altair, from Shrewsbury, N. J , a distance of about five miles from the place where they landed. When our Collector left the vessel, yesterday afternoon, she had fifteen feet water in the hold, and it was supposed she had her hack broke, and that the mainmast had gone through her bottom. She lies nearly head on, and the water was making a breach over her midships.

The ship will it is feared fie a total loss. f She is worth from 865,000 or $70,000- Most of the cargo will probably be saved in a damaged state, its invoice value is about £72.000 sterling þÿ $35 000 is insured on the vessel The amount insured on the caigo is not known, hut there is certainly not one half covered in this city.

From the New York Herald, January 16. State of the þÿCountry Finance ami Morals. The extraordinary spectacle was presented yesterday of the stock oi the United States Bank selling for 47 per cent, which about t-vo or three years ago sold for 120 to 125. The stockholders, many of whom are f males, will lose two thirds of their property. This strange and unprecedented fact is only one taken from series on series, happening all over the country, developing the charlatanism and demoralization which prevail over a large portion of financial and political society. In addition to this spectacle, it is stated in our correspondence from Baltimore, that the hanks of that city will not resume, and that the principal cause for the adoption of this policy has been created by the wants oi the State for a new loan. By these tinholv bargains between the politicians and the financiers, all morals and honesty þÿ all sound doctrine and practical sense are set at naught, and cast aside. The various States want more money þÿ and the hanks want more time þÿ hence the one gives and the other takes, leaving the burden upon the people, in the shape of taxes, at some distant dav. In congress the same principle of demoralization seems to prevail. That body are about to pass laws to divide the landed property of the nation among the several states þÿ and also a law for the abolition of all debts, under the name of a bankrupt law, excluding corporations.

By reference to our advertising columns, it will be seen that a new line of steam packets is to be formed immediately between this port and Havana, to leave on the 5th and 15th of each month. The first steam packet to leave this port under the arrangement will he the Clarion, which is to be hauled up to day at the Dry Dock, for the purpose of having a steam engine and Ericcson's patent propellets inserted in her. This movement will form an entirely new era in steam navigation. The great advantage that the Clarion will have over other vessels are these: þÿ she can proceed on her voyage in a calm as well as a gale; she can pump herself out if leaky, at the rate of 150 men power per hour; she can also, if struck by lightning, and set on fire (like the Poland) drown the fire out in a very short time, bv her powerful engine. Again, furnished with the propelling power, she will always he sure of stays in heating of! a lee shore in heavy weather, when other vessels will have to ware. And, lastly tfie speed of the ship under close reefed top sails and courses, on the wind, in a heavy sea, and going at the rate of five miles per hour, can fie increased to eight, more or less, at the discretion of the commander. Should we thus succeed in successfnll combining steam power with canvass, we shall

for fuel. Modern steam ships, with paddles larboard and starboard, are liable to power, ful objections ; when the ship is under a heavy press of canvass, and rather light on the wind, she heels over at an angle of 45 degrees ; this brings the lee wheel under water, and the weather one out, consequently the whole propelling power is lost. But on Ericcson's plan, a ship's way in that state, would not he checked, because her two propellers under her stern, would be constantly urging her forward The Clarion will only require to have two small holes cut in her stern, for the propellers . and her engine put in ; and will be ready for sea by the 5th of February next. We look with great anxiety for the result, and are pleased to find that the enterprising projectors have taken out a patent right for this invention both in Europe and this country ; and a Canadian company have purchased the right to use it on our extensive Northern lakes.

Latest from Buenos Ayres add Rio Janeiro. þÿ By an arrival at Baltimore, intelligence from Rio, to Nov. 25th, has been received. That which we published exclusively a day or two since is confirmed. The British packet Spider, from the River La Plata, arrived at Rio de Janeiro, on the 24lh, and brought official intelligence that the difficulties between the French and Buenos Ayrean Governments had been settled on terms satisfactory to both parties þÿ that the blockade had ceased þÿ and the Bueno sAvres was again open to commerce The U. S. ship Marion, Captain Belt, was at Rio de Janeiro, having just arrived from Montevideo. She had been run on shore in the La Plata, on the English bank, by a pilot, and was afterwards got of bv throwing overboard some of her guns. They were, however. afterwards recovered, and the ship supposed not to be very materially injured.

Our Relation t with Great Britain. þÿ We learn from the Richmond Erquirer that, iq the new aspect assumed by our relations with Great Britain, in consequence of the reeenl þÿ lowering correspondence between Mr, Forsyth and Mr. Fox in the case o! the Caroline, the President has requested Mr. Stevenson to waive his own wishes, and remain in London until his successor should arrive þÿ provided one should be appiontcd early after the new administration goes into power, and provided he should leave the United States shortly after his þÿappointment. We do not imagine that Mr Stevenson wii,f be embarrassed by any delay tn the selection of his successor. His services are not so essential that they cannot be dispensed with ; and we presume that there will be no difficulty in designating a minister at least equally þÿ entitled to the confidence of the country þÿ Mr. þÿFox, the Enquirer, has put which will never be yielded, until every drop of American blood has been þÿ poured forth a claim, which it will require þÿ all the dimness and wisdom of the administration to prevent running into some misþÿ chief. We have even most serious fear . þÿ þÿ upon all our decision and discretion we may be the occasion ; and we wish, that with prevent a dark and bloody result þÿ such is the arrogant spirit of the British þÿ Government, and such are the questions now þÿ at issue between the two þÿcountries, Mr. Ritchie appears unusallv and unnecessarily belligerent. His friends are determined that the new administration shall not

lack embarrassments, if it is in their power to accumulate them. We have not witnessed so much Loco Foco gallantry as Mr. Ritchie exhibits, any time for the last ten years He absolutely thirts for carnage ; and talks of pouring out blood as indifferently as if it was only so much haid cider. If Mr. Kitchif. reads the debates in Congress, he must have learned by ihis time that the statesmen likely to stand high in (he confidence of the new admuiistrution do not indulge in those goomy forebodings. In an incidental debate which occurred in the Senate on the 8th inat., on the Boundary Question Mr. Clay declared that he considered the idea of the probability of a future rapture with Great Britain entirely unfounded. He was not disposed to put himself in a passion, because Mr Fox had used strong language in his correspondence, without instructions from his government. We have no fears that there will be any want of firmness and wisdom> in this matter, or in any other that may fall under the direction of Mr. Webster, in the Department of State. His gigantic energies will be devoted to the preservation of the peace, as well as the honor of the country There will he no idle gasconade in his oego. ciations. He will assume no tone of insolent bravado, for the puerile gratification of giving point to a diplomatic correspondence. petent to an? exigencies of peril or warfare-the same gallant soimer will give direction to our affaira, who conducted our North west nt army on its career of danger and glory, arid who war never yet defeated in fighting the battles of hia country.

Mr, Ritchie may spare his vaticinations, and quiet his anxieties. The responsibility of bringing the country into difficulty may rest upon himself and his friends. The responsibility of extricating it, the American people have confided to other hands.

France and Buenos Ayres --We have been favoured with a Rio de Janeiro paper of the 25th November, containing a copy of the Treaty of Peace recently concluded between the French Admiral and the Government of B uenos Avres. A friend has kindly furnished a translation of it, which shall be published in to morrow's American. The news that ihe Treaty had been concluded produced, it appears, a great sensation at Montevideo. All the French residing there protested against the act, and resolved to draw up a petition to be sent to the French Chambers. The Dictator Francia of Paraguay died on the 20th ol September last. A junta of five members had suceeded him in the Govern- j incut. Cava lie had obtained, it was said, a new triumph over Paehecoi and tins General, as well as Oribe and Marscarillas, fled towards Buenos Ayres.

The money, cotton, and othei markets have all improved. The war party has been completely put down in Fi ance ; and on the whole, the news is highly encouraging, and promises peace and prosperity. The Allies have taken St. Jean þÿd Acre, blew it up in grand style, and have, in short

order, completely used up poor old Mehemet A ! i and Ibrahim, who now says its no use þÿ lie will give up the fleet, give up Syria, and simply agree to the Pacha of Egypt. O G U UGIVE T A F U I C II A R D II A T C II h T T . that the Allies were still willing to leave him the Government of Egypt, provided he surrendered at once the Turkish fleet and withdrew his army from Syria. The Bey replied that he was willing to give up the Turkish fleet and withdraw his remaining army from Syria, when he should be officiallv advised that the Grand Senior had revoked his decree depriving him of the Government of Egypt and declaring him an outlaw. Napier replied that the conditions he asked must be acceded to bv the Bey within 24 hours, or the bombardment of Alexandria would commence. The Bey, in consequence signed and concluded a treaty with Commodore Napier to withdraw his troops from Syria, and to send to Ibrahim, his Son. by a British Steamer, orders to that effect. Also to give up the fleet as soon as it could be made ready ; Napier promising on the part of the Allies that the conditions relative to the Bey's retaining the þÿGov of t, Egypt should be complied with. Thus has the whole Egyptian war been triumphantly brought to a close in a very short time by the gallantry of Commodore Napier, and bv his very efficient and skilful services both by sea and land ; and with cornparitivelv, a handful of European troops þÿ he planned and executed the whole proceedings in Syria aided bv the valor of the fleet and of the marines under his command.

S. annual message to Congress; our limits not permitting longer quotations Those now made relate to the foreign concerns of the Government; þÿ The residue of the message principally refers to the local affairs of the nation, with a long dissertation on the advantages of the subtreasury law, and against the establishment of a National bank.
From the N. Y. Enquirer, December 11, 1840. EXTRACT FROM THE MESSAGE
FROM THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES. TO THE TWO HOUSES OF CONGRESS.

Our devout gratitude is due to the Supreme Being for having graciously continued to our beloved country, through the vicissitudes of another year, the invaluable blessings of health, plenty, and peace. Seldom has this favored land been so generally exempted from tiie ravages of disease, or the labor of the husbandman more amply rewarded ; and never before have our relations with other countries been placed on a more favorable basis than that which they so happil) occupy at this critical conjuncture in the affairs of the world. A rigid and persevering abstinence from all interference with the domestic and political relations of other I your separation. These were promlly con- States, alike due to the genius and distinct- j sidered ; such as were deemed correct in ive character of our Government, and to the principles bv which it is directed ; faithful j to the just rights of the United States aiid of a observance, in the management of our foreign j the state ot Maine, concurred in; and the relations, of the practice of speaking plainly, dealing jnstiy, and requiring truth and justice in return, as the best conservatives of the peace nations ; of a strict impartiality in our manifestations of friendship, in the commercial privileges we concede, and those we requite from others : these, accompanied by a disposition prompt as to maintain, in every emergency, our own rights, as we are from principle averse to the invasion of those of others, have given to our Country and Gov-

einmonla standing in the great family of nations, of which we have just cause to be proud, and the advantages of which are experienced by our citizens throughout every pot lion of the earth to which their enterpri" sing and adventurous spirit may carry them. Few. any, remain if insensible to the value of our friendship, or ignorant of the terms in which it can be acquired, and by which it can alone be preserved. A series of questions of long standing, difficult in their adjustment, and important in their consequences in wftich the rights of our citizens and the honor of the country were deeply involved, have, in the course of a few years, (the most of them during the successful administration of mv immediate predecessor,) been brought to a satifactory conclusion ; and the most important of those remaining. are, 1 am happy to believe, in a fair wa v of being speedily and satisfactorily adjusted. With all the Bowers of the world our relations arc those of honorable peace. Since your adjournment, nothing serious has occurred to interiupt or threaten this desirable

1BJ&1T31E TssvisnBSss ma«3iaaaif03 atjt harmony. If clouds have lowered above the other hemisphere, they have not cast their portentions shadows upon our happy shores. Bound by no entangling alliances, yet linked by a common nature arid interest with the other nations of mankind, our aspirations are for the preservation of peace, in whose solid and civilising triumphs all may participate with a generous emulation. Yet it behoves us to be prepared for any event, and to be always ready to maintain those just and enlightened principles of national intercourse, for which this Government has ever contended. In the shock of contending empires, it is only by assuming a resolute bearing, and clothing themselves with defensive armor> that neutral nations can maintain their rights, The excitement which grew out of the terj ritorial controversy between the United States and Great Britain having in a great measure subsided, it is hoped that a favorable period is approaching for its final settlement. Both Governments must now be convinced of the dangers with which the question is fraught ; and it must be their desire, as it is their interest, that this perpetual cause of irritation should be removed as speedily as practicable. In my last annual message you were informed that the proposition for a commission ol exploration and survey promised by Great Britain had been received, and that a counterproject, including also a provision for the certain and final adjustment of the limits in dispute, was then before the British Government for its consideration.
The answer of that Government, accompamed by additional propositions of its own, was received, through its minister here, since

principle, and consistent with a due regard reasons for dissenting from the residue, with an additional suggestion on our patt, communicated by the Secretary of State to Mr. Fox. That minister, not feeling himself sufficiently instructed upon some of the points raised in the discussion, felt it to be his duty to refer the matter to his own Government for its further decision. Having now been for some time under its advisement, a speedy answer may be confidently expected. From the character of the points still in difference and the undoubted disposition of both parties to bring the matter to an early conclusion, I look with entire confidence to a prompt and satisfactory termination of the negotiation. Three commissioners were appointed shortly after t he adjournment of congress, under the act of the last session providing for the exploration and survey of the line which separates the states of Maine and New Hampshire from the British Provinces ; they have been actively employed until their progress was interrupted by the inclemency of the season, and w ill resume their labors as soon as practicable in the ensuing year. It is understood that their respective examinations will throw new light upon the subject in controversy, and serve to remove many erroneous impressions which may have been made elsewhere prejudicial to the rights of the United States. It was, among other reasons, with a view of preventing the embarrassments which, in our peculiar system of government, impede and complicate negotiations involving the territorial rights of a
State, that I thought it my duty, as you have been informed on a previous occasion, to pro-

pose to the British Government, through its minister at Washington, that early steps should be taken to adjust the points of difference on the line of boundary from the entrance of Fake Superior to the most northwestern point of the Lake ol the Woods, try the arbitration of a friendly Bower in conformity with the seventh at tide of the treaty of Ghent No answer has yet been returned by the British Government to this proposition. With Austria, France. Prussia, Russia, and the remaining Powers of Europe, I am happy to inform you our relations continue to be of the most friendly character. With Belgium, a treaty of commerce and navigation, based upon liberal principles of reciprocity and equality, was concluded in March last, and, having been ratified by the Belgian Government, will be duly laid before the Senate þÿ It is a subject of congratulation that it provides for the satisfactory adjustment of a longstanding question of controversy ; thus removing the only obstacle which could obstruct the friendly and mutually advantageous intercourse between the two nations. A messenger lias been despatched w ith the Hanoverian treaty to Berlin, where according to stipulation, the ratifications are to be exchanged þÿ I am happy to announce to you that after many delays and difficulties, a treaty of commerce and navigation, between the United States and Portugal, was concluded and signed at Lisbon, on the 26th of August last, by the Plenipotentiaries of the two Governments.

Its stipulations are founded upon those principles oi mutual liberality and advantage which the United States have always sought to make the basis of their intercourse with foreign Powers, and it is hoped they will tend to foster and strengthen the commercial intercourse of the two countries.

The Niantic reports that the American ships Adelaide and Washington had been stopped at the Bocca Tigris, when coming out. by the blockading squadron then under command ot Captain Warren, of the Volage. Application for their release was made to Captain Smith, then at Macao, who ordered the ships to the anchorage at Capsut moon, and promised that the case should be immediately investigated. We have received, by an extraordinary courier, letters from our correspondent in Alexandria of the 2d iust , and from Malta of the 5th inst. and brought by the Meteore and another steam vessel (name not given) to Marseilles, where they arrived on the 12th inst. It appears, from these letters and journals, that the Euphrates arrived at Alexandria on the 30th ult. but took the ground on entering that harbour, which retarded for some time the delivery of her despatches þÿ The intelligence from Syria states, that a large force of the allies, consisting of between 10.000 and 12,000 men, was proceeding to attack Ibrahim in the plain. He is said to have 15,000 men under his command. The former was composed of 5,000 Turks, 4,000 Syrian mountaineers, and 1,500 English þÿ « On the result of the impending þÿengagement, say our letters, depenus the fate of the cam- þÿ piign. The rumoured spirit of disaffection in the army of Ibrahim is, however, for lum a menacing affair, and would render the issue of the contest in no respect þÿdoubtful. The same paper (the Malta Times) states that a Greek vessel, which arrived in that island on the 3d, stated that he parted company on the 2d, with the French fleet of eleven sail of the line, off Cape Passaro on its return to Toulon. Independently of our own despatches, we find in the Semaphore de Marseilles a private letter dated Alexandria, Nov. 1, which states that the last accounts from Syria were more favourable for Mehemet A ! i ; that the moun-

taineers were becoming dissatislied with their new allies, in consequence of the departure of the Emir Bechir, the sending of the prison" e s taken from Ibrahim to Constantinople, and the removal of the mountaineeis who had declared for the Sultan to points remote from them.

The Semaphore repeats that the new Emir with 5,000 Turkish troops, 4,000 mountaineers, and 1,500 English (the latter under the orders of Commodore Napier in person) and marched to attack Ibrahim, who had 15.000 men in the plain. The correspondent states that the operations before St. Jean d'Acre had ceased, or had not been commenced, for the want of adequate means to carry on a siege. The place was said to be very strong on the sea side, but, infinitely more strong on the side of the land, Soliman Pacha, who had been ill of fever, had left to have an interview with Ibrahim.

The Malta Times mentions a rumour that, on the contrary, Acre had fallen into the hands of the allies: but this report seems to require confirmation ; for a private letter, from a most respectable quarter in Alexandria, informs us that Admiral Stopford left Bey rout on the 2(>th of Oct. with two sail of the line, to bombard that place. þÿ »oOo- - From the Barbadian, December 10, 1840.

The late accounts from Syria state that Sir Charles F. Smith, now a Major General with local rank, ha 1 recovered his health, and had returned from Constantinople with the appointment by the Sultan of Commander in Chief of the '1 urkish forces in Syria.

A Memorandum has been read at the head of the Regiment, 11th Hussars, bv the adju taut General of the Army, by order of Lord Hill, Commanding in Chief, in which there is much implied censure on the officers, and especially on Lord Cardigan, the Colonel, in consequence of the frequent disputes in the Regiment, and the late duel. The Morning Chronicle remarks thus ; þÿ According to Lord Hill, the conduct of Lord Cardigan has been ungentlemanly, and without moderation, tern per and discretion, yet Captain Reynolds, whose conduct has been the necessary etiect of that of the Earl of Cardigan, is made the victim. No wonder that the public should be excited from one end of the country to the other. VVe are absolutely overwhelmed with communications ; and from what we learn the whole Army is in commotion. It would have been better not to have been so careful in selecting officers for the courtmart al, capable of uttering a dictum which has excited the disgust of all men of gentlemanly feeling throughout the þÿkingdom. We publish to day a letter from Captain Reynolds to the Editor of the Chronicle, which we intended on Wednesday, but bad not room for it. It is a most honorable specimen of the Captain's gentlemanly feelings, and of his candour and loyalty.

Whether civil or military officers, soldiers or people, whosoever shall be able to take an English man-of-war, carrying 80 great guns delivering the same to the þÿmandarins shall receive the reward of 20,000 Spanish dollars. For a smaller vessel, carrying fewer gnns< less will be given, for every great gun less the reward will be diminished 100 dollars. Whatever the vessel contains besides the great guns, weapons of war and opium, which must be given up to the mandarins, excepting such as clocks, watches, cloths, goods, or money, all these in addition shall be awaided to ihe takers of the vessel ! Again, to anv who shall destroy a great man of war of the said foreigners, not leaving a single planksubstantial evidence being produced of the same, shall be given the reward of 10,000 dollars ; for a smaller one less in proportion ! 2. Whether large or small, for the destrovitgor sinking of each English vessel, substantial evidence being produced of the same, the proportion of one third of the foregoing rewards shall be awarded. 3. For taking alive a foreign mandarin, or offic/'r, on inquiry should it be ascertained that he is the said man of þÿwai chief s officer, the reward shall be 5,000 Spanish dollars ; tor anv other officer, more or less accm ding to his rank and office; the rule lessening for þÿevery degree lower, the reward shall be diminish! d 500 Spanish dollars. 4. ATHlMFr TO BURN TUB BRITISH FLEET. The Clinton Register gives the following account of another attempt to burn the Bri tish fleet, on the 9<h June, at Capsingmoon þÿ The first alarm was given about two a. m on Tuesday. A noise was heard from among the small Chinese boats on shoie. It appeared, on subsequent inquiry, that some mandarin boats had got in amongst them for the purpose of making captures. They attacked the cutter Devil, and wounded some of the Lascars on board. Immediately after, distant lights appeared in the direction of the passage of the Capsingmoon, called the Flood Gates ; and the commanding officer of the Danish King fired a gun and hoisted the signal previously ordered by the senior ofli cer of her þÿMajesty ships s for fire rafts ; and, instantly almost, the fire burst forth from at least fifteen fire boats ; the appearance was very beautiful. The wind and tide were then favorable for their course- As they approached, they blew up like some beautiful works, what in English pyrotechnical science would be called a flowerpot. The beauties of the sight, however, did not dissipate the a- j larm felt by those on board the ships, who were also fearful of other crafty schemes in progress ; consequently most of the ships slipped their cables and moved out of danger, each more anxious than his neighbour to get into tlie rear. The scene and danger caused great excitement ; the night was very dark, the wind slackened, and so many vessels being under weigh at once in a small space, oc-

casioned great confusion, and many consequently came in contact, but we have not heard of any serious damage. The boats ol the squadrons were activelv employed towing the rails clear of the shipping, and anchoring others. The junks were first turned adrift, chained together two and two; nine of these rafts were counted, which gives eighteen boats But it was ascertained that some had not ignited, and some h.id exploded, the wrecks being seen floating about the buy the next morning. On examination the fire rafts were found to be constructed of very old outside fishing boats, filled with combustible matter of all descriptions What remains of them will supply the shipping with fire-wood for a month. They were full of dross, the remains of the combustible matter. The fleet did not suffer any damage from those rafts, as most of them were speedily towed on shore by the boats of the squadron.

From the London (iazette, Tuesday, Dec. 1. FOREIGN -OFFICE, Nov. 30. A despatch, of which the following is a copv, has been received at this office, addressed to Viscount I'almerston. G. My Lord þÿ On the 20th ult. it was finally determined between Sir Robert Stopford and myself that the siege of Acre should be undertaken. 1 accordingly detached Omar Bev for the purpose of advancing from Sidon with 2000 Turks upon Tvre, and thence to oecupy the Pass of the White Mountain, to the northward of this place ; and on the 31st the Yd niral made sail from Beyrout Roads, having previously embarked in the squadron 3.0 tt) men. under the immediate command of the PnshnJSelim, and small detachments of Rovitl Artillery and Sappers under Major lliggins. of the former corps, and Lieutenant Aldrich, Royal Engineers. Omar Bey reached the position assigned to Itim at the same hour on the second instant that the fleet appeared off Acre. Owing to the light winds the ships did not gel into action till 2 P. From the French Papers. ARRIVAL OK THE ItEM AINa' OK NAPOLEON AT CHERBOURG. I he Belle Poule frigate, commanded by the 1 rittce de Joinviile, and which has brought hack to J ranee the remains ol the Emperor Napoleon, came to anchor at Cherbourg, on the 30th ult. at five in the morning. I he following is the report of his royal highness to the Minister ot Marine. " Monsieur le þÿMinistre As i had the honor of informing you, I quitted All Saints' Bay on September 14, running along the coast of j Brazil, with the wind at east, but which, having veered to the north and north east, enabled me quickly to gel into the meridian of Saint Helena, without having to pass the twenty-eight south parallel. On entering this meridian, 1 was delayed by caltns and i light breezes. On October 8, 1 came to art anchor in James Town roads. The brig Oreste, detached by Vice Admiral de Mackau to bring to the Belie Poule a pilot from the channel, had arrived the day before. As this ship brought me no new instructions, I immediately occupied myself in executing the orders I had originally received. My first care was to put M. de (Jhabot, the Kings Commissioner, in communication with General Middlemorc, governor of the Island. These gentlemen having settled, according to their respective instructions, the manner of proceeding to the exhumation of the remains of the Emperor Napoleon, and their translation on board the Belle Poule, October 15, was fixed for the execution ot their plans. The Governor

charged himself with the exhumation, and all that was to take place within the British territory. J, by the order of October 13, a copy ol winch 1 hereto annex, regulated the honors to be paid on the 1 5th and Kith by the division under my command. The French merchant ships, the Bonne Amie, Captain Gallet, and Indien, Captain Truquetil, eagerly rendered their assistance. At midnight on the ' 15th the operation commenced in t he presence ol the French and English commissioners, M. do Chabot and Captain Alexander, ol the Roy a! Engineers. The works were directed by the latter. As M. do Chabot renders to the government a circumstantial account of the operations to which he was a witness. J conceive that 1 am dispensed from entering into the same details, and shall content myself with saying that at ten in the morning the coffin was found in the grave.

- þÿ After having raised i< in fact, it was open ed, and the body was found in an unhoped for state of preservation. At th s solemn mo« rrient, at the sight of the easily recognised remains of him who had done so much for the glory of France, the emotion was deep and unanimous. At half past 3 o'clock, the guinj of the fort announced to the ships and vessels in the roadstead that the fnnera! procession had commenced its march towards James Town. The militia and the troops of the garrison preceded the ear, which was covered with a pall, the corners being borne by Generals Bertrand and Gourgaud, and Messrs De l.acases and iMarcband, the authorities and a crowd of the inhabitants following. The guns of the frigate having answered those of the fort, she continued to fire minute guns. From the morning the yards were slung and the flags hoisted half-mast high, as signs of mourning, in which foreign ships and vessels joined. When the process, on appeared on the quay, the English troops formed a double line, through which the car passed slowly to the shore. At the water's edge, where the English lines had terminated. Iliad collected all the officers of the French dtvision, waiting, in deep mourning and heads uncovered, the approach of the coffin When within twenty paces of us it slopped, and the Governoi advancing to me, delivered up to me, in the name of his government, the remains ol the Emperor Napoleon. As soon as the coffin was lowered into the boat of the frigate prepared to receive it, the

general emotion was again renewed þÿ the dying wish of the Emperor Napoleon began tobe accomplished þÿ his remains reposed under the national flag All sign of mourning was from that time abandoned, the same honors which the Emperor would have received had he been living, were paid to his mortal remains. and it was amidst salutes from the ships, dressed out in their jcolors, and their yards manned, that the 'cutter, escorted by the boats of all tho ships, pursued its way slowly towards the frigate. By the arrival of the Schooner Grand-Canal direct from Mayaguez, lelteis have been received confirming the news of the destructive fire which entirely ruined the town of Mayaguez on the 30th of last month, as we announced it in our paper of the 6th instant The loss which that place has sustained by that disastrous conflagration is considerable, being estimated at 2 millions of dollars ; more than 20,000 quintals of cuflee, it is said, have been destroyed, for as no price had as yet been fixed for that article it remained in town in the hands of shop keepers, to he subsequently conveyed to the playa when sold. The consequences of that lamentable occurrence were, that trade and business were at once thrown into the greatest stagnation, Which will last for some time; a serious delay will also, of course, be occasioned in payments, which will most prejudicially re-act upon the merchants of our Island, who have large outstandings in the hands of the shopkeepers in town as well as amongst the merchants on the playa- The former being entirely ruined, as it appears that nothing lias been saved, are unable to pay either the merchants here or those on the plava to whom they were largely indebted, and as the piincipal resources of the latter are derived from the shop keepers in town, they will find themselves in some difficulty to meet their engagements in this Island. We have no data by which we could value the extent of the outstandings of our merchants here amongst those on the playa and in the town

of Mayaguez. but judging bv what we have heaid, we can estimate it at from 350, to 400,000, dollars. Although the accounts which have as yet reached us are all distressing in the extreme, yet we have heard ft om good authority, that a considerable portion of the amount due by the merchants on the plava, will be shortly received ; the utifortu nate shopkeepers who have been in a great measure left destitute, will require longer indulgence. We have not the least doubt, that our merchants, who are alive to the voice of humanity, will come forwuid to assist those who deserve that a helping hand should be stretched to them, by rendering to them such facilities as may restore to them and their helpless families the comforts of life that were blasted within a few hours. It was in the afternoon of the 30th last, that the fire commenced ; the feeble efforts which were made to arrest its progress proved entirely unavailing; in tact such was the rapidity and unconquerable power ol the fire, that 'he whole town was reduced to ashes within the short space of 8 hours! The pillage which such a scene of confusion encouraged, increased the distress of the whole community. It is impossible for us to form a correct idea of the rapidity with which that prospering place has been mined and of the manifold miseries which its devoted inhabitants have suffered and are still suffering; those alone who have witnessed the fires of St. Thomas and all the misfortunes consequent to them, will be able to picture to themselves their

heart renting calamities. There perished in a few hours a town for the inhabitants of which we wish to express our heartfelt sympathies; its former prosperity, we fear, will not dawn again, at least not in a short time, unless the j government of the Island come to its relief, and we are very far from supposing that it i will abandon or be parsimonious to a place,

V\ e recollect at this moment the fatherly feelings which the present Governor of that Island expressed in his first proclamation to its inhabitants, when he assumed the reigns of tha' government ; arid we have observed with great satisfaction, that his arrival in Mayaguez, which took place shortly after the fire, was attended with acts of benevolence and humanity. May bis protecting hand w iselv contribute to relieve the distress of those who are entrusted to fiis particular care, and to cause Mayaguez to arise again from her ashes with renewed vigour and greater prosperity.

IMPORTANT NEWS FROM EGYPT. The subjoined intelligence from Alexandria, dated the 21st hist, and published in second and third editions by our morning contemporaries, created a great stir in the city this morning, as the first impression made by it was that Admiral Stopford's refusal to ratify Commodore Napier's treaty with Mehemet Ali, was tantamount to a total rejection of the treaty by the Four Powers This impression was happily erroneous; for scarcely had Admiral Stopford, acting upon his individual sense of duty, refused to ratify the treaty, when Lord Palmerston, evidently without being aware cf the existence of Commodore Napier's Convention, authorized the Admiral to propose a treaty for Mehemet Ali's accept-
ance, the same m tenor and in substance as

n 1 1 » þÿ i þÿw»w þÿm m p iki > wwin i in 'mm that alreadv signed by the Commodore. This is a most flattering testimony of the wisdom of the course pursued by Commodore Napier. In fact, the only difference between the treaty of Lord Palmerston and the treaty of Commodore Napier is, that the former allows only three days for the restoration of the Turkish fleet, while the latter permitted the Viceroy to retain it till the Porte had revoked the sentence of deposition and confirmed his Highness in the government of Egypt. Mehemet Ali has accepted Lord Palmerston's treaty, and thus the Eastern question is happily in a state of speedy and amicable adjustment. This affords us tiie gi eater pleasure, us for the lust ten days the war party in France; and the Tory press of the Metropolis, having been circulating rumors ot the rejection of Commodore Napier's convention by the lour powers, andol their secretly abetting the determination ot the Porte to carry out the sentence of deposition, lhese rumors were repeatedly contradicted in our columns, and our readeis will now see on belter authority than any of the my sterious correspondents of the Times, the Post, and the Herald. It is to be regretted that Admiral Stopford, who was aware that Commodore Napiei s Tieatv was despatched direct to England from Alexandria trie day it was signed, and consequently would be iu the hands of Lord Palmeiston almost as soon as in his own, did not think it proper to await instructions from England, before refusing to ratify it. His

abrupt rejection of the Treaty was a severe censure of the conduct of one of the bravest officers that ever trod a quarter deck, and at the same time was calculated to impress the Viceroy with a conviction that lie was shamefully tiifled with by England. At the same time that Mehemet Ali learned the refusal of Admiral Stopford to ratify the treaty, he received an overland despatch from his son Ibrahim, stating that he and his entire army in two divisions were in full letreat on Egypt.
